<jats:p>Purpose - As one of the great inventions of modern society, the company system is an important driving force for social progress. As a malpractice in the operation of the company, the deadlock of the company is harmful to the company itself, its shareholders, creditors and even the public.
Design/Methodology/Approach - The judicial dissolution system in Article 183 of China’s current Company Law provides a legal basis for judicial intervention in the deadlock of the company and fills the legislative gap. Yet the corporate stalemate is not simply linked to judicial dissolution (Bao Weimin, 2005). Corporate deadlock is only one of the reasons why shareholders have the right to request judicial dissolution; judicial dissolution should not be the only solution to the deadlock.
Findings - Forcing the dissolution of the company to resolve the deadlock is clearly wrong for shareholders who want to resolve the deadlock but do not want to destroy the company.However, China’s current Company Law provides too single judicial remedy, too general regulations and weak operability.
Research Implications - This paper discusses the extension and connotation of corporate deadlock and analyses the rationality of judicial intervention (Wang Jianjian, 2013). This paper also analyzes the concept and characteristics of the company deadlock, and provides a standard for the determination of the company deadlock, limits the environment of the company deadlock to limited liability company and further limits the scope of the discussion.</jats:p>
title: A Study on Judicial Intervention in China’s Corporate Impasse: Focusing on the Application of Judicial Dissolution of a Company

items.abstract: <jats:p>Corporate exit and corporate vitality are complementary rather than contradictory. A sound exit regime should therefore distinguish firms that ought to leave the market from firms that remain viable and should be rescued. This article argues that the principle of corporate survival and development should operate as a binding constraint on the design and judicial application of corporate exit rules in China. To contain the spillover risks of exit, the law should require warranted exit, orderly exit, transparent exit, and rational exit. Courts should adopt a survival-anddevelopment-friendly adjudicative philosophy: invalidate incorporation only with great caution and favor cure of defects; favor composition over liquidation, reorganization over liquidation, and merger over dissolution. Grounds for invalid incorporation should be narrowly confined, remediable defects should be cured before invalidity is declared, and a judgment of invalid incorporation should not retroactively unsettle lawful transactions with bona fide counterparties. In corporate-deadlock litigation, dissolution should be a last resort after courts have exhausted less destructive alternatives, including inspection rights, damages, compulsory dividends, share transfers, shareholder exit, and corporate division. Bankruptcy law should likewise preserve viable corporate life. Courts should be permitted to presume that a debtor company is eligible for reorganization, subject to rebuttal, and should consider debtor-inpossession or corporate self-governance where internal governance remains functional. Reorganization should also encourage entrepreneurship, respect commercial practice, and incorporate the business judgment rule. Finally, China should develop rescue procedures tailored to small and micro enterprises and coordinate company law, bankruptcy law, and related legislation around a common commitment to corporate survival, sustainable development, creditor protection, and market discipline.</jats:p>
title: The Principle of Corporate Survival and Development as a Binding Constraint on Corporate Exit Invalid Incorporation, Judicial Dissolution, and Bankruptcy Reorganization in China

items.abstract: <jats:p><p>The foremost principle of company law should be to respect and protect a company’s rights to survival and development, thereby promoting corporate continuity and sustainable development. This principle is designed to enhance corporate vitality, protect market entities, and reduce the number of zombie companies. It forms part of public order and good morals; legal acts contrary to it should therefore be invalid. The principle should be stated in the General Provisions of the Company Law and should permeate the entire body of company-law rules and the whole corporate life cycle. Corporate registration should be reconstructed around improving corporate survival rates and competitiveness. To safeguard the company’s interest in sustainable development and prevent the company from suffering when self-governance fails, shareholder derivative litigation should be activated, valuation adjustment mechanism (“VAM”) clauses entered into by the target company should be held invalid, and companies should in principle be prohibited from guaranteeing the debts of others. The core of corporate governance lies in strengthening the company’s capacity for sustainable development. Adjudication in dissolution, bankruptcy, and invalid-incorporation cases should seek to preserve the company wherever possible. Dissolution actions arising from corporate deadlock should, as far as possible, be resolved through mediation. Administrative regulation and sanctions should likewise be designed to promote sustainable corporate development. Listed companies and the natural persons who actually commit violations should be subject to differentiated accountability so as to avoid inflicting a “second injury” on public investors. Criminal accountability for entrepreneurs should be pursued without sacrificing the survival of otherwise innocent companies. The center of gravity of market regulation should shift from products to corporate governance.</p></jats:p>
title: The Principle of Corporate Survival and Development as a Binding Constraint on Corporate Exit Invalid Incorporation, Judicial Dissolution, and Bankruptcy Reorganization in China

items.abstract: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>Corporate judicial dissolution was formally introduced into Chinese Company Law in 2005, and yet there has been scant academic research exploring the function and implications of this procedure. This paper aims to rectify this by offering a comprehensive empirical study of the practice. Research shows that the procedure has been increasingly exercised by shareholders, though the total number of such cases is relatively small. The research also revealed many flaws in the procedure, which is not surprising; teething troubles are all but inevitable for a new procedure. The study also reveals that the courts do not strictly follow the relevant provisions of the Company Law and Judicial Interpretations when adjudicating judicial dissolution cases. Instead, Chinese judges appear to have created their own specific rules, a practice that runs counter to China's current legal system. Finally, this article proposes that the shareholder oppression could be introduced and enacted as one of the grounds to initiate the judicial dissolution.</jats:p>
title: Corporate judicial dissolution in China

items.abstract: <jats:p>Partisan polarization has infected our politics at levels not seen in decades. But what happens when the contamination spreads to the institutions responsible for regulating the political process itself? At the Federal Election Commission, nothing. Under the FEC’s governing statute, the Federal Election Campaign Act, any serious action the agency undertakes must be supported by a bipartisan supermajority of commissioners. When the six commissioners fail to reach such consensus—or “deadlock”—due to partisanship or otherwise, nothing happens at all: no investigations, no regulations, no enforcement of federal campaign finance laws. For the first few decades of the FEC’s existence, these deadlocks were mostly harmless, if still frustrating. Thanks to FECA, even inaction by the FEC was subject to a critical safeguard: judicial review. But since 2018, the D.C. Circuit has found Heckler v. Chaney to bar review of deadlocks in which the commissioners voting against an enforcement action invoke the agency’s prosecutorial discretion. Consequently, a non-majority bloc of commissioners can refuse to support any or all enforcement proceedings—even for entirely partisan purposes—with little to no judicial oversight, simply by referencing the agency’s discretion in their reasoning. <br><br>This Article attempts to resolve this stalemate by proposing a framework to guide judicial review of these deadlock dismissals. Based on the Chevron “Step Zero” of United States v. Mead Corp. and its foundation in legal process principles of institutional competency, this two-part framework limits Chaney’s preclusion of review to agency actions that carry the “force of law.” Because FEC deadlock dismissals represent a failure of the Commission to speak authoritatively as a whole, they do not carry the force of law, and thus are reviewable. For these and other agency actions that fail this “Chaney Step Zero,” the framework also provides a less absolute but still deferential inquiry to evaluate the persuasiveness of the agency’s invocation of its discretion—a prosecutorial-discretion analogue of Skidmore v. Swift. While this framework is designed to combat the gridlock plaguing the FEC, its principled and organized approach to Chaney’s application has the potential to guide judicial review of discretionary action throughout the administrative state.</jats:p>
title: Chaney Step Zero: Judicial Review of FEC Deadlock Dismissals

items.abstract: The Concentrate Questions and Answers series offers the best preparation for tackling exam and assignment questions. Each book includes key debates, typical questions, diagram answer plans, suggested answers, author commentary and tips to gain extra marks. This chapter deals with divorce, dissolution, separation orders and judicial separation and contains a mixture of essay and problem questions. The first question is a problem question that considers the ground and facts for divorce contained in the Matrimonial Causes Act 1973 and the equivalent provisions of the Civil Partnership Act 2004. The second is a problem question that also requires students to apply the law of divorce, but further necessitates consideration of judicial separation. The third and fourth questions are essay questions that focus on reform of divorce law and the use of mediation in divorce proceedings.

items.abstract: <jats:p>This article discusses the remedy of judicial dissolution in the context of an Illinois corporation facing management deadlock. The particular focus of this article is on one of the most common corporate structures for small businesses: the equally-held firm where management rights are symmetrical with ownership interests. Although courts long have described dissolution as an extreme and disfavored remedy, they have done so without reference to the particular factual context unique to deadlocked closely-held corporations. Illinois has a unique shareholder-relief statute, which illustrates when dissolution is an appropriate remedy. Based on the statutory text, I suggest dissolution is a default remedy in deadlock cases when a petitioning shareholder does not request a buy-out of her shares in the litigation and when the corporation’s shareholders have failed to include deadlock avoidance mechanisms in their advance planning documents. As support, I demonstrate the motivations for why a shareholder in an equally-split firm may eschew a buy-out remedy altogether and prefer dissolution.</jats:p>
title: Dissolution and Rational Choice: The Unique Remedial Framework for Director Deadlock under the Illinois Business Corporation Act
Corporate Governance Deadlock

items.abstract: Each Concentrate revision guide is packed with essential information, key cases, revision tips, exam Q&As, and more. Concentrates show you what to expect in a law exam, what examiners are looking for, and how to achieve extra marks. This chapter focuses on divorce, dissolution, and judicial separation as means of ending marriage or civil partnership. It first considers the grounds for divorce/dissolution and highlights five facts that can be used to prove a marriage has irretrievably broken down: adultery, behaviour, desertion, two years’ separation with consent, and five years’ separation. The chapter then compares no-fault divorce with divorce based on fault and provides an overview of the Family Law Act 1996 and considers mediation as a way to resolve these sorts of disputes. Finally, it examines mediation as an alternative to the court process when dealing with divorce, dissolution, and judicial separation.
title: 3. Divorce, dissolution, and judicial separation

items.abstract: <jats:p>The literatures on non-market strategy in business studies and the thematically intersecting field of lobbying and interest group research in political science both exhibit a profound blind spot when it comes to how corporate influencing unfolds in relation to the judiciary and the broader justice system (henceforth corporate judicial activity - CJA). <br><br>There are many prima facie plausible reasons why not to bother with the judiciary when it comes to corporate political activity. All of these justifications however turn out to be misguided – ontologically, conceptually, practically. Quite to the contrary, current political and legal dynamics suggest that the judiciary has evolved into a pivotal area of concern and engagement for corporate political activity and lobbying more generally. <br><br>CJA is at a minimum highly interdependent with and complementary to conventional modes of exerting influence on executive and legislative functions. But, more often than not, shaping the justice system represents the ultimate prize, where successful interventions come with a deeply structural impact. Successfully influencing the judiciary hard-codes special privileges into the system of interest politics that transcend the benefits achievable through other political strategies<br><br>What’s more, the practical CJA repertoire can be deployed in ways that evade public scrutiny to a surprising extent and exploit glaring, yet largely overlooked loopholes in the ethics and integrity infrastructures that are idiosyncratic to the judicial apparatus. <br><br>An organizing framework centred around the four thematic “containers” of ideas, institutions, people and events can provide a first good template for cataloguing different types, practical manifestations and empirical characteristic of CJA in a systematic way. Cataloguing these examples underscores that CJA is not just standard corporate political activity exercise in just another domain but comes with a number of highly distinctive features and dynamics<br><br>Principal among these is the observation that at the vortex of CJA sits an influencing industry made up of big law firms that serve as super-agents who can potentially reap even bigger benefits from influencing successes than their clients. They are more highly incentivised, much better resourced and less heavily regulated than conventional lobbying firms.<br><br>In sum, one cannot understand the contemporary role of business in politics without considering the role of business action in the justice system. And one cannot contemplate possible implications for corporate responsibility and effective policy reforms without such an enlarged focus that includes CJA.</jats:p>
title: Corporate judicial activity
